name: Haudenosaunee religion

dating.dating_summary: Material correlates of ceremonial practice generally (Ontario Iroquoian ossuary reburial tradition, ~1000-1300 CE) predate the earliest outsider written attestation (1636, and even that is Huron/Wyandot-recorded, a related but distinct Iroquoian confederacy, not Six-Nations-specific); the Confederacy's founding and the core religious/political narrative's composition are dated anywhere from 1142 to 1600 CE by different named scholars using incompatible methods, with no consensus resolution, and the tradition's own position declines to fix a date at all ("time immemorial").

earliest_archaeological_evidence.note: Ontario Iroquoian ossuary (communal reburial) tradition, interpreted archaeologically as reflecting the ceremonialism later described ethnographically as the Feast of the Dead (Ohgiwe). This dates a ceremonial correlate generally, not the specific creation narrative or Great Law content.

earliest_written_attestation.note: Jesuit Relations (Reuben Gold Thwaites, ed., 1896-1901 compilation), 1636 volume, records the name "Ataentsic" for a foundational sky-being — but this attestation is from Jesuit missionaries among the Huron/Wyandot, a related but historically and politically distinct Iroquoian confederacy, NOT one of the Six Nations. The earliest Six-Nations-specific outsider documentation is later and was not pinned to an exact date in this research pass.

surviving_manuscript_date.note: Seth Newhouse's ~1880-1885 Mohawk-to-English manuscript of the Great Law (not formally chiefs-approved); standard published English version edited by Arthur C. Parker (Seneca ethnologist), 1916.

estimated_composition.method: No single agreed scholarly date; treated by sources as effectively the same contested question as the Confederacy's political founding.

tradition_internal_claim.note: The Haudenosaunee Confederacy's own official position states the League has existed since "time immemorial," declining to fix a calendar date.

estimated_oral_origin.method: No defensible independent linguistic-dating method (e.g. glottochronology) was located for the oral tradition's transmission depth, distinct from the eclipse-astronomy method (Mann and Fields) or the archaeological-settlement method (Snow) used to date the founding event itself.

notes: Category tags reflect: polytheism/animism (Sky Woman, the Twins, and a broader cosmology of named beings), ancestor_veneration (Feast of the Dead/Ohgiwe), mixed. The 19th-century Longhouse Religion (Gaihwi:io, founded by Handsome Lake beginning 1799) is a documented, relatively recent religious REFORM movement explicitly combining older Haudenosaunee tradition with selected Christian influences in response to post-Revolutionary-War social crisis (land loss, alcoholism) — not ancient tradition; see claim_handsome_lake_longhouse_reform. A strict "good vs. evil" moral-binary reading of the Twins (Sapling/Flint) shows likely Christian missionary overlay in some recorded 19th/20th-century versions (including apparent virgin-birth imagery); in less-Christianized tellings the Twins are paired complementary forces (day/night, life/death) with a relationship of rivalry rather than strict villainy, and Flint functions as a trickster rather than a devil-figure.
